name: Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
summary: Choose models, knowledge architectures, retrieval, chunking, and prompt governance.

topics.title: RAG vs. fine-tuning vs. prompting
topics.rule: Separate changing knowledge from changing behavior and changing instructions.
topics.question: A manufacturer runs a support assistant on Amazon Bedrock. Its private product manuals are stored in Amazon S3 and updated every day. Answers must reflect the latest approved manual and identify the source passage. The team wants to minimize ongoing model-training work. The application already follows the requested response style, but previously correct answers become stale after source updates. A prompt-only prototype cannot access the private manuals. The source set fits the supported managed ingestion path. Which solution best meets these requirements?
topics.clue: Daily document updates and source attribution require current evidence at inference time.
topics.why: Use Bedrock Knowledge Bases to index the approved manuals and retrieve relevant passages for each question. Retrieval supplies the changing facts and source references without retraining model weights for every update. Keep ingestion synchronized so the retrieved evidence actually reflects the latest approved manual.

options.name: Bedrock Knowledge Bases — RAG
options.when: Answers need external/current evidence with attribution.
options.trap: RAG still needs current indexes, correct retrieval, and access controls.
options.action: Synchronize approved S3 documents into Bedrock Knowledge Bases and retrieve source passages for each generated answer.

options.name: Bedrock model customization — fine-tuning
options.when: An evaluated stable behavior/style need justifies updating supported model weights.
options.trap: Fine-tuning is not a live document-refresh mechanism.
options.wrong: Daily fine-tuning adds the training work the team wants to avoid and does not itself provide passage-level evidence for each answer.
options.action: Fine-tune a supported Bedrock model on each approved manual update and rely on the customized model for source facts.

options.name: Bedrock Prompt Management — prompting
options.when: Instructions, examples, formatting, and reusable templates need refinement.
options.trap: A template does not fetch missing private facts.
options.wrong: Manual titles and instructions do not supply the private passages needed to answer or cite the question.
options.action: Version the system prompt in Prompt Management with manual summaries and retain the existing prompt-only request path.

options.name: Bedrock response caching
options.action: Store generated answers in a question-keyed cache and extend cache lifetime to reduce calls after document updates.
options.when: Reuse a scoped answer while its evidence and configuration remain valid.
options.trap: A cache must be invalidated when relevant source versions change.
options.wrong: Reusing answers after a manual update can return outdated facts; a cache is not the source-refresh mechanism.

flow: Amazon S3: approved manual versions
Bedrock Knowledge Bases: synchronize and retrieve relevant passages
Amazon Bedrock: answer using those passages
Response: include and verify source references
topics.change: If the evidence is already supplied and the remaining problem is consistent terminology or response style, test prompt changes and then consider supported fine-tuning.

topics.title: Managed Knowledge Bases vs. custom RAG
topics.rule: Check whether the managed feature meets the requirement before building the whole pipeline.
topics.question: A team is building an S3-backed assistant with Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Its selected vector store and citation requirements are supported. A document-specific chunking routine can run within the Knowledge Bases Lambda transformation contract. The team needs this routine while minimizing ownership of ingestion and retrieval. The routine preserves section boundaries and adds source metadata; it does not require an unsupported search algorithm. The team can maintain this one Lambda function, but does not want to operate independent index synchronization and citation handling. Which approach should it choose?
topics.clue: The custom processing fits a managed extension; the rest of the managed pipeline already meets the requirements.
topics.why: Configure custom chunking through the supported Lambda transformation and keep Knowledge Bases responsible for the remaining ingestion and retrieval stages. The requirement is a specific extension, so replacing the entire RAG pipeline would create unnecessary ownership.

options.name: Knowledge Bases + Lambda transformation
options.when: Managed RAG features fit, with supported custom chunk/metadata processing.
options.trap: Managed does not mean automatic entitlement or automatic source freshness.
options.action: Use a Knowledge Bases Lambda transformation for the chunking routine and keep managed embedding, indexing, and retrieval.

options.name: Custom RAG pipeline
options.when: Required ranking, query behavior, or stage control is unsupported by managed features.
options.trap: Custom chunking is not by itself proof that managed RAG cannot fit.
options.wrong: A custom pipeline can perform the routine, but adds synchronization and citation ownership when a supported managed extension meets the stated requirement.
options.action: Implement the chunking routine in a new Lambda/OpenSearch RAG pipeline and take ownership of synchronization and citations.

options.name: Answer-stage prompt processing
options.when: Refine how an answer uses evidence already retrieved.
options.trap: Answer formatting cannot define ingestion-time chunk boundaries.
options.wrong: Post-retrieval processing cannot change the document units that were embedded, so the required section boundaries are absent from ingestion.
options.action: Keep default Knowledge Bases ingestion and apply the section-boundary routine to the context after retrieval.

options.name: Expanded retrieval context
options.action: Keep default indexing and increase retrieved context until the document-specific sections are included in the model prompt.
options.when: Additional retrieved passages supply evidence missing from the current context.
options.trap: More context does not implement custom ingestion-time chunk boundaries.
options.wrong: Larger retrieval context may contain more material, but it does not implement the specified chunking routine and metadata contract.

flow: Amazon S3: document input
AWS Lambda transformation: produce the required chunks
Bedrock Knowledge Bases: embed and index transformed chunks
Knowledge Bases retrieval: supply passages and source references
topics.change: A custom RAG pipeline becomes appropriate when required query, ranking, or ingestion behavior cannot be implemented by the managed service and its supported extensions.

topics.title: Embedding dimensions and model fit
topics.rule: Compare quality and cost within the actual embedding model contract; dimensions are not an accuracy guarantee.
topics.question: An OpenSearch vector index uses 1,024-dimensional Titan Text Embeddings V2 vectors for documents and queries. Storage cost is increasing. The team wants to evaluate smaller vectors while preserving an agreed retrieval-recall target. The existing index is healthy and a labeled query set establishes the baseline recall. There is no evidence of an ingestion failure. Any new configuration must use a consistent embedding model and vector size for documents and queries. Which plan is technically valid and gives evidence for the decision?
topics.clue: Reduce vector size while keeping document and query embeddings compatible and measuring retrieval quality.
topics.why: Titan V2 supports 256, 512, and 1,024 dimensions. Build separate compatible test indexes for the smaller configurations and use matching query vectors on the same held-out questions. Compare recall and storage before selecting a configuration; vector size alone does not establish quality.

options.name: Titan V2 supported dimensions
options.when: Choose among supported V2 dimensions using workload measurements.
options.trap: Lower dimensions can affect quality; storage savings are not the whole bill.
options.action: Build 256- and 512-dimensional Titan V2 test indexes with matching query vectors and compare held-out recall and storage.

options.name: Titan G1 embeddings
options.when: Evaluate a different embedding model with a compatible rebuilt corpus and query path.
options.trap: Model migration must meet the same retrieval and storage goals.
options.wrong: G1 is a different embedding model and its larger vectors do not meet the stated smaller-vector storage objective.
options.action: Switch to 1,536-dimensional Titan G1 vectors for both documents and queries, then migrate after measuring recall.

options.name: Query/corpus compatibility
options.when: Queries and indexed vectors use compatible embedding spaces and dimensions.
options.trap: Document and query vectors must use a compatible embedding space and dimensions.
options.wrong: The query vectors cannot be compared with the existing document vectors at a different dimension.
options.action: Keep the 1,024-dimensional document index and issue 256-dimensional query vectors to reduce per-query vector size.

options.name: Unevaluated dimension reduction
options.action: Generate 256-dimensional document and query vectors with Titan V2 and deploy them after confirming indexing succeeds.
options.when: A smaller supported configuration meets the measured quality target.
options.trap: Successful ingestion does not prove acceptable retrieval recall.
options.wrong: The dimensions are supported and compatible, but indexing success does not establish that the required recall target is preserved.

flow: Held-out questions: define the recall target
Titan V2: create matching document and query vectors
OpenSearch test indexes: compare 256 / 512 / 1,024 dimensions
Decision: select a configuration that meets quality and cost targets
topics.change: If smaller vectors fail the recall target, retain the higher-dimensional configuration or evaluate other embedding and retrieval choices on the same test set.

topics.title: Fixed, semantic, and hierarchical chunking
topics.rule: Choose chunking for document structure and retrieval needs, then measure it.
topics.question: A Bedrock Knowledge Base indexes long maintenance manuals in a vector store that supports hierarchical chunking. Evaluations show that short passages match specific fault codes well, but the answer often needs the surrounding section to interpret safety conditions. The team wants to match narrow passages and supply their broader section context. Increasing retrieval result count has added unrelated sections without reliably restoring the condition attached to each match. The team wants a managed ingestion change and must keep the returned context smaller than the entire manual. Which ingestion strategy best fits?
topics.clue: The matching unit should be small, while the returned context should include its surrounding section.
topics.why: Hierarchical chunking indexes child passages for focused matching and replaces retrieved children with their parent context. This directly connects narrow fault-code matches to the surrounding conditions the answer needs. Evaluate the additional context against the token budget.

options.name: Hierarchical chunking
options.when: Structured documents benefit from focused child retrieval and broader parent context.
options.trap: Returned parent context consumes tokens and can change result counts.
options.action: Configure supported hierarchical chunking so focused child matches are returned with their broader parent context.

options.name: Fixed-size chunking
options.when: Predictable simple splits meet the measured evidence requirement.
options.trap: A hard boundary can separate a condition from its claim.
options.wrong: Larger fixed chunks can add context, but change the matching unit rather than providing the requested small-child matching with parent-context return.
options.action: Increase fixed-size chunk length until each returned chunk contains more of the manual around a fault code.

options.name: Semantic chunking
options.when: Meaning-based boundaries improve results on the tested corpus.
options.trap: It is not always best and does not imply parent substitution.
options.wrong: Semantic chunking can create coherent passages, but does not supply the specifically requested child-to-parent expansion.
options.action: Use semantic chunking to form coherent topic passages and return the matched passage without parent expansion.

options.name: No chunking
options.action: Disable chunking so retrieval supplies the complete manual containing the matching fault code.
options.when: A small self-contained document can be retrieved as one unit.
options.trap: Large documents can weaken focused matching and consume excessive context.
options.wrong: A complete long manual exceeds the required bounded section context and loses the focused matching unit.

flow: Maintenance manual: section and safety conditions
Knowledge Bases ingestion: create parent and child chunks
Retrieval: match the focused child passage
Model context: return the broader parent section
topics.change: If coherent independent passages already contain all required conditions, fixed-size or semantic chunking may meet the requirement with less surrounding context.

topics.title: Vector vs. hybrid vs. reranking
topics.rule: Retrieval collects candidates; reranking reorders candidates it actually receives.
topics.question: A Bedrock assistant uses an OpenSearch vector index of equipment manuals. The AX-1047 manual is current, authorized, and contains the correct instructions. For “pressure issue on AX-1047,” semantic search returns other pumps and omits AX-1047 from the candidate set. Increasing candidate count has not reliably recovered this literal identifier. Inspection confirms that ingestion and tenant filtering are correct. The team wants to improve retrieval without retraining the generator or weakening access controls. Which change best addresses this observed failure?
topics.clue: The correct source is absent from retrieval candidates, despite being indexed and accessible.
topics.why: Add a lexical or exact-ID retrieval signal alongside semantic search so AX-1047 can enter the candidate set. The failure occurs before reranking and generation; those stages can only use evidence they receive. Evaluate candidate recall before changing the generator.

options.name: OpenSearch lexical / vector retrieval
options.when: Literal identifiers and semantic intent both need to influence candidate selection.
options.trap: Hybrid support/configuration matters; it is not universally higher quality.
options.action: Add lexical equipment-ID matching alongside vector search and evaluate whether AX-1047 enters the candidate set.

options.name: Bedrock reranking
options.when: The relevant evidence is already in a broad candidate set but poorly ordered.
options.trap: A reranker cannot recover a document absent from its input.
options.wrong: A reranker can reorder existing candidates, but AX-1047 is not in the input set.
options.action: Use a Bedrock reranker to reorder the current semantic candidate set before context selection.

options.name: Bedrock generation model
options.when: Generation capability is the measured bottleneck with adequate evidence.
options.trap: A stronger model cannot supply a missing private passage.
options.wrong: The larger model still receives other manuals rather than the private AX-1047 instructions.
options.action: Use a larger Bedrock model to interpret the symptom while keeping the same candidate retrieval path.

options.name: Inference parameter tuning
options.action: Lower generation temperature and require an AX-1047 citation while keeping the same retrieved passages.
options.when: Tune sampling when generation variability is the measured defect.
options.trap: Sampling parameters do not retrieve an omitted private source.
options.wrong: More consistent generation does not correct the missing retrieval candidate.

flow: User question: AX-1047 plus the pressure symptom
OpenSearch: combine literal-ID and semantic candidate retrieval
Candidate check: confirm the AX-1047 passage is present
Amazon Bedrock: answer from the selected authorized passage
topics.change: If AX-1047 enters the candidate set but ranks below irrelevant passages, reranking becomes a reasonable next experiment.

topics.title: Prompt Management vs. Flows vs. workflow
topics.rule: Template governance, visual prompt chains, and durable business orchestration have different owners.
topics.question: Three applications invoke Amazon Bedrock using shared prompt templates. Releases must identify the exact template version, variable definitions, and model configuration used. The team wants centralized template management and reproducible releases. Each application currently copies prompt text into its code, so template changes require three separate releases and past evaluations are hard to reproduce. No long-running approval wait or multi-node invocation chain is part of this requirement. Which capability is the most direct fit?
topics.clue: The shared resource is a versioned prompt template and its invocation configuration.
topics.why: Bedrock Prompt Management stores reusable templates, variables, and supported configuration, and creates versions that applications can reference. This supplies a common released prompt resource rather than introducing a new runtime workflow. Evaluate a version before promoting it.

options.name: Bedrock Prompt Management
options.when: Store and version prompt templates and their configuration.
options.trap: A saved version is not evidence that it passed review or evaluation.
options.action: Publish shared prompt resources and approved versions through Bedrock Prompt Management and reference them from the applications.

options.name: Amazon Bedrock Flows
options.when: Connect supported prompt, knowledge, tool, and condition nodes.
options.trap: Orchestrating nodes is a different requirement from a template repository.
options.wrong: Flows connect execution nodes; the stated requirement is governance of reusable prompt resources, not a node execution chain.
options.action: Create a Bedrock Flow for each application and keep prompt definitions separately inside those flow nodes.

options.name: AWS Step Functions
options.when: Own durable steps, retries, waits, and controlled business actions.
options.trap: Do not add durable execution state without a workflow need.
options.wrong: Execution history records a process run, rather than managing the shared prompt template and released variants.
options.action: Record prompt text in Step Functions execution inputs and use execution history to reproduce prior application releases.

options.name: Invocation logging
options.action: Enable model invocation logging and use logged requests to reconstruct the prompt configuration used by each application.
options.when: Use invocation logs to inspect supported model interactions.
options.trap: Observed requests are not a governed template repository.
options.wrong: Logs help investigate calls, but do not manage reusable templates and release versions.

flow: Shared template: variables and model configuration
Bedrock Prompt Management: create a released version
Release evaluation: approve the version
Applications: reference the approved prompt version
topics.change: Use Bedrock Flows when the requirement becomes a supported visual chain of prompts, retrieval, and conditions; use Step Functions for durable business steps and waits.

name: Implementation and Integration
summary: Distinguish agents, workflows, MCP hosting, model deployment, API delivery, and shared gateways.

topics.title: Agents and frameworks vs. Step Functions
topics.rule: Ask who chooses the next action: the model or developer-defined workflow states.
topics.question: An application processes contracts stored in Amazon S3. Every contract follows a defined sequence: extract text, run two checks, obtain a lawyer’s approval, then create a case through an API. Approval can take several hours. Failed checks must be retried individually without restarting completed steps. The case API can safely handle an idempotency key. The checks may invoke Bedrock, but the model must not choose the process order or bypass approval. The team needs a record of the state reached by each contract. Which component should own this process?
topics.clue: The sequence is predetermined and must retain execution state across a long approval wait.
topics.why: A Step Functions Standard workflow can represent the fixed states, retry failed tasks, and wait for an approval callback. Bedrock can perform the bounded model checks inside that workflow. The orchestration requirement is durable state and explicit control flow, rather than model-selected actions.

options.name: Step Functions Standard
options.when: Known control flow must survive waits and partial failures.
options.trap: Durability does not make repeated external writes safe without idempotency.
options.action: Use Step Functions Standard task states, scoped retries, and a callback approval state before the idempotent case write.

options.name: Bedrock Agents
options.when: An FM must decide which permitted tool/action comes next from observations.
options.trap: Fixed steps do not require model-selected autonomy.
options.wrong: Conversation context is not the durable workflow and callback mechanism needed for the prescribed approval process.
options.action: Use Bedrock Agents action groups for extraction, checks, and case creation, with approval progress held in conversation context.

options.name: Agent frameworks
options.when: Custom agent logic or specialist coordination is required.
options.trap: Framework choice does not replace deterministic approval/authorization.
options.wrong: Specialist coordination does not itself supply durable execution state and per-step recovery for the fixed process.
options.action: Coordinate specialist agents in an agent framework and use their conversation transcripts to resume the contract process.

options.name: Long-running Lambda
options.action: Run the sequence in Lambda and keep the invocation waiting until the lawyer responds before creating the case.
options.when: Use Lambda for bounded tasks within a process.
options.trap: A Lambda invocation is not an hours-long approval wait.
options.wrong: The approval can exceed Lambda execution limits and keeps a task running instead of persisting a durable wait.

flow: Step Functions Standard: start the contract execution
Extraction and Bedrock tasks: run the defined checks
Approval callback: wait for the lawyer’s decision
Case API task: create the approved case with idempotency protection
topics.change: An agent becomes appropriate when the next permitted tool or action genuinely depends on model reasoning over observations, rather than a known sequence.

topics.title: Synchronous vs. streaming vs. asynchronous
topics.rule: Separate complete-response delivery, incremental delivery, and background job completion.
topics.question: A writing assistant calls Amazon Bedrock through an API Gateway REST API and Lambda. The current path buffers the complete answer. Users accept the total generation time but want text to appear as it is generated. The selected model and integrations support streaming. Traces show neither initialization delay nor model throttling. The user must remain in the writing session, and the application must retain its authenticated REST API entry point. Which change best meets the user requirement?
topics.clue: The target is earlier visible text, rather than a longer timeout or later job completion.
topics.why: Use ConverseStream and forward its output through Lambda and the API Gateway streaming integration without collecting the full answer first. This exposes generated text while generation continues. Increasing the timeout still returns one completed answer; a background job changes the interaction instead of delivering a live stream.

options.name: ConverseStream / InvokeModelWithResponseStream + streaming transport
options.when: Interactive users benefit from incremental output.
options.trap: Streaming does not inherently reduce total inference work or token cost.
options.action: Use ConverseStream and forward output through Lambda and the API Gateway REST streaming integration as it arrives.

options.name: Converse / InvokeModel with a longer buffered timeout
options.when: The consumer needs the complete response before acting.
options.trap: A bigger timeout does not expose partial tokens.
options.wrong: The response remains buffered until generation completes, so the first visible text does not arrive earlier.
options.action: Retain Converse and buffered Lambda output, but increase the API Gateway integration timeout for longer responses.

options.name: SQS → worker → stored asynchronous result
options.when: The caller can accept a job ID and complete later.
options.trap: Background completion is not incremental output to a waiting writer.
options.wrong: A job ID fits deferred completion, but it does not deliver the requested live generated text in this session.
options.action: Queue requests in SQS, return a job identifier, and let the client retrieve the completed answer from a result endpoint.

options.name: Lambda concurrency tuning
options.action: Increase Lambda reserved concurrency and preserve the existing buffered model-response integration.
options.when: Use concurrency controls to address execution admission and capacity.
options.trap: Concurrency does not change response delivery semantics.
options.wrong: More concurrent invocations do not make a single buffered answer visible before completion.

flow: Bedrock ConverseStream: produce incremental output
Lambda: forward events without full-response buffering
API Gateway REST API: stream the integration response
Client: display text as it arrives
topics.change: If the caller can leave and collect the result later, an SQS-backed asynchronous job is appropriate; if it needs one short complete answer, buffered synchronous delivery may suffice.

topics.title: Bedrock capacity vs. SageMaker hosting
topics.rule: Deployment follows capacity and hosting controls, not merely whether weights are customized.
topics.question: A team has a fine-tuned model artifact and a compatible serving container. Its deployment must use a chosen GPU instance family, expose the container’s runtime configuration, and scale the endpoint’s instance count with demand. The model has already passed its quality evaluation. The constraint comes from its runtime dependencies and hardware selection, rather than a need for cross-Region capacity. The team accepts responsibility for endpoint deployment and capacity management. Which AWS hosting option best meets these requirements?
topics.clue: The decisive requirements are serving-container, GPU-instance, and endpoint-scaling control.
topics.why: A SageMaker AI real-time endpoint exposes the model/container and instance configuration and supports endpoint autoscaling. Choose it because those hosting controls are required. Having customized weights alone would not establish the choice, because eligible custom models can also be used in Bedrock.

options.name: SageMaker AI real-time endpoint
options.when: Serving container, supported instance/GPU selection, and endpoint scaling are decisive.
options.trap: Owning an endpoint adds capacity, deployment, and operations responsibilities.
options.action: Deploy the compatible container and artifact to a SageMaker real-time endpoint with selected instances and endpoint autoscaling.

options.name: Bedrock on-demand
options.when: Managed model inference without endpoint instance management fits.
options.trap: Eligible imported/custom models exist; hardware control is still a separate boundary.
options.wrong: Managed Bedrock inference avoids endpoint operations, but does not expose the selected GPU fleet and serving-container configuration required here.
options.action: Use an eligible Bedrock custom-model on-demand deployment to avoid managing a serving endpoint.

options.name: Bedrock Provisioned Throughput
options.when: Supported models need reserved, measured sustained model capacity.
options.trap: Reserved Bedrock capacity is not a user-chosen SageMaker GPU fleet.
options.wrong: Reserved model throughput addresses capacity planning, not the required container runtime and endpoint instance-count controls.
options.action: Reserve supported Bedrock model capacity with Provisioned Throughput to handle sustained inference demand.

options.name: Bedrock cross-Region inference
options.action: Use a supported Bedrock cross-Region inference profile to distribute requests across eligible regional model capacity.
options.when: Use supported profiles to route inference across eligible Regions.
options.trap: Regional routing does not expose hardware or container management.
options.wrong: Broader regional inference capacity does not supply the requested GPU/container hosting controls.

flow: Model artifact and container: define the serving runtime
SageMaker endpoint configuration: select supported GPU instances
Real-time endpoint: serve requests
Endpoint autoscaling: adjust the eligible instance count
topics.change: If managed model inference meets the runtime requirements and the team does not need instance/container control, evaluate an eligible Bedrock deployment and its capacity options.

topics.title: Lambda vs. ECS for MCP servers
topics.rule: Choose hosting by tool runtime, duration, dependencies, and service lifecycle.
topics.question: An agent uses two MCP tools. One tool is a CPU-based service that maintains connections across calls and must remain continuously available. The other performs a short stateless lookup in DynamoDB and has intermittent demand. The team wants to avoid maintaining a service fleet for the lookup. Both tools use supported CPU runtimes and can store durable data outside process memory. A conversation session may call either tool several times, and its durable state is stored in DynamoDB. Which hosting design best fits?
topics.clue: One tool requires a persistent service lifecycle; the other is a bounded stateless operation.
topics.why: Host the persistent CPU tool in an ECS/Fargate service and the short lookup handler in Lambda. This assigns each tool the runtime it needs while avoiding a continuously running fleet for the lookup. Store durable business state in DynamoDB rather than relying on handler memory.

options.name: ECS / Fargate + Lambda
options.when: Different runtime profiles justify separate hosting choices.
options.trap: Check runtime support; GPU/host-specific needs can require another compute choice.
options.action: Host the persistent CPU tool as an ECS/Fargate service and run the intermittent stateless lookup handler in Lambda.

options.name: Lambda execution environment
options.when: Bounded stateless tool handlers fit Lambda.
options.trap: Invocation memory is not a continuously available durable service contract.
options.wrong: External data is appropriate, but Lambda environment reuse does not guarantee the continuous service/connection lifecycle required by the persistent tool.
options.action: Run both handlers in Lambda, externalize session data in DynamoDB, and depend on environment reuse for connection persistence.

options.name: ECS services
options.when: A persistent runtime is needed and service operations are justified.
options.trap: External DynamoDB state alone does not force containers.
options.wrong: Both tools can run in containers, but the lookup then retains the service fleet the team wants to avoid.
options.action: Host both handlers as ECS services and externalize their durable session data in DynamoDB.

options.name: Fargate task per call
options.action: Host the lookup in Lambda and invoke a new short-lived Fargate task for every call to the persistent tool.
options.when: A bounded container task needs a supported runtime without a persistent service.
options.trap: Container technology alone does not establish the required service lifecycle.
options.wrong: Fargate supports the runtime, but launching a fresh task for each call does not maintain the required continuously available tool service.

flow.start: MCP client: route calls to the requested tool
branches: ECS / Fargate: maintain the persistent CPU tool service
AWS Lambda: execute the short lookup on demand
flow.end: Amazon DynamoDB: hold durable business data outside handler memory

topics.change: If both handlers become short stateless operations, Lambda can fit both; if the lookup gains a persistent runtime requirement, reconsider container hosting.

topics.title: Q Business vs. Q Developer vs. custom Bedrock
topics.rule: Distinguish an enterprise assistant, developer productivity, and an application you build.
topics.question: An organization evaluating the services in the exam blueprint wants a packaged employee assistant over supported enterprise document sources. It requires identity-aware access, built-in connectors, and conversational answers with source citations. The team prefers a managed application over building its own assistant. The sources include supported internal document repositories rather than software source-code assistance. Employees must receive only content their identity permits. There is no requirement for a bespoke business transaction workflow or GPU-serving configuration. Which service best matches this category?
topics.clue: The requirement is a packaged enterprise knowledge assistant with connectors and citations.
topics.why: Amazon Q Business is the enterprise-assistant category described here. It packages the document-connector and employee question-answering experience, whereas a Bedrock application requires the team to build that experience. Q Developer addresses developer productivity rather than this employee knowledge task.

options.name: Amazon Q Business
options.when: Packaged enterprise search/chat over supported organizational sources fits.
options.trap: Exam scope and availability for new deployments are separate questions.
options.action: Configure Q Business with supported document connectors and employee identity-aware access.

options.name: Amazon Q Developer
options.when: Developers need supported coding, review, transformation, or IDE help.
options.trap: Developer productivity is not the employee knowledge-assistant requirement.
options.wrong: Q Developer is oriented to developer tasks; it is not the packaged enterprise document assistant requested.
options.action: Configure Q Developer for employee questions and use its developer-assistance experience as the document assistant.

options.name: Custom application using Amazon Bedrock
options.when: Custom UX, integration logic, or business workflow control is required.
options.trap: Building the application adds responsibility and development.
options.wrong: A custom Bedrock assistant can be a valid architecture, but adds application work when the scenario explicitly prefers a packaged solution.
options.action: Build a custom employee frontend and retrieval/application logic around Bedrock Knowledge Bases.

options.name: SageMaker AI hosting
options.action: Host a model on SageMaker and implement custom connectors, retrieval, permissions, and the employee frontend.
options.when: Use an endpoint when model hosting controls are required.
options.trap: Model hosting alone does not implement enterprise search and application features.
options.wrong: An endpoint still needs connectors, retrieval, identity-aware application logic, and a user experience.

flow: Employee identity: establish authorized access
Q Business connectors: ingest supported enterprise sources
Q Business assistant: retrieve permitted evidence
Employee response: answer with source citations
topics.change: Choose a custom Bedrock application when bespoke interaction or business integration requires control beyond the packaged assistant. Check current service availability before a real deployment.

topics.title: GenAI gateway vs. direct invocation
topics.rule: A gateway centralizes shared admission, routing, accounting, and policy; a direct path stays simpler when these are unnecessary.
topics.question: Five teams invoke Bedrock from separate applications. The platform team must enforce team-specific model access and token admission, attribute usage to each team, and change model routes without client releases. Clients already have authenticated identities. API request-rate limits are already in place, but equal request counts produce very different token usage. A route change should be deployed once by the platform team, and clients must not be trusted to enforce their own entitlements. Which architecture most directly supplies a consistent shared enforcement point?
topics.clue: Several applications need centrally enforced admission, attribution, and model routing.
topics.why: Place an application gateway/router behind API Gateway and derive team policy from trusted identity. The router checks entitlement and token admission before invoking Bedrock and records attributed usage. AppConfig can provide deployed routing configuration; policy enforcement remains application logic at the shared boundary.

options.name: GenAI gateway: API Gateway + Lambda/router + accounting
options.when: Multiple applications need shared model policy and controls.
options.trap: API request throttles and budget alerts alone are not hard token-spend enforcement.
options.action: Use a shared API Gateway/application router with trusted team identity, enforced token admission, attribution, and AppConfig model routes.

options.name: Direct unrestricted Bedrock credentials in each client
options.when: A simple trusted application needs no additional shared gateway boundary.
options.trap: Direct clients can bypass centralized admission unless controls are otherwise enforced.
options.wrong: This can implement policies per application, but lacks the required common enforcement boundary and routing changes independent of client releases.
options.action: Give applications direct Bedrock access and require each team to release its own entitlement, token, and routing implementation.

options.name: AWS Budgets notifications as the admission system
options.when: Spending thresholds require notifications or supported budget actions.
options.trap: Budget alerts are not per-request real-time token admission.
options.wrong: Tags and budgets help attribution and spending oversight, but do not enforce per-request model entitlement or token admission.
options.action: Use tagged direct Bedrock calls and team budgets to provide attribution and notify teams when they approach spending limits.

options.name: API throttling
options.action: Centralize calls behind API Gateway request-rate throttles while leaving token decisions and model routes in client releases.
options.when: Use throttles to control request admission rates.
options.trap: Request count and token consumption are different units.
options.wrong: Request throttles help rate control, but do not enforce token admission; client-owned routes still require client releases.

flow: API Gateway: accept an authenticated request
Shared router: derive team identity and enforce entitlement/token admission
AppConfig routing configuration: select the permitted model route
Amazon Bedrock invocation: record team-attributed usage
topics.change: For a single trusted application without shared routing or admission requirements, direct model invocation may be the simpler sufficient path.

name: AI Safety, Security, and Governance
summary: Separate content safety, access, PII location, audit evidence, governance ceilings, and threat detection.

topics.title: Guardrails vs. IAM vs. Lambda validation
topics.rule: Content policy, AWS permissions, and deterministic business rules are distinct controls.
topics.question: A Bedrock agent can call a refund tool implemented in Lambda. A policy allows refunds only to the authenticated customer’s account and up to that customer’s approved amount. The model can propose an account ID and amount. The proposed request is valid JSON, and the tool role can reach the refund service. However, the same role serves many customers, and an amount allowed for one customer may be unauthorized for another. Harmful-content filtering is already enabled. Which design best enforces these transaction-specific restrictions?
topics.clue: The proposed values must be checked against trusted customer identity and approved business data for every write.
topics.why: Validate the account and amount in the Lambda handler or authoritative refund API before executing the write. IAM should limit which resources the handler can access, and Guardrails can apply content policy, but neither replaces the customer-specific transaction checks. Treat the model’s proposal as untrusted input.

options.name: Lambda / authoritative refund API
options.when: Schemas, customer scope, amount limits, and side effects must be enforced in code.
options.trap: A prompt instruction is not the transaction authority.
options.action: Validate customer ownership and the approved amount in the Lambda/refund API before executing under a scoped service role.

options.name: Bedrock Guardrails
options.when: Supported content/topic/PII/grounding policies need filtering.
options.trap: Content safety does not implement every business entitlement or money rule.
options.wrong: Content filtering does not verify that this account belongs to this caller or that this amount is approved.
options.action: Keep the shared tool role and use a Bedrock Guardrails policy to reject refund requests outside the stated business policy.

options.name: IAM permissions
options.when: AWS service actions and resources need least-privilege access.
options.trap: Application-specific transaction rules still need an enforcing business boundary.
options.wrong: An API permission grants access to an operation; it does not by itself compare proposed values with this customer’s business rules.
options.action: Scope the shared Lambda role to the refund API and execute schema-valid proposals under that IAM role.

options.name: Prompt instructions
options.action: Include the authenticated customer policy in the agent prompt and accept proposals that satisfy the output schema.
options.when: Prompts communicate expected behavior to the model.
options.trap: Valid structure does not prove authorization or valid business values.
options.wrong: Instructions and a valid schema cannot enforce the trusted per-transaction checks at the write boundary.

flow: Bedrock agent: propose refund parameters
Lambda / refund API: verify customer, account, amount, and approval
Authorized write: execute under a narrow service role
Refund result: record an idempotent transaction outcome
topics.change: If the question concerns access to an AWS API or resource, IAM is the relevant control; if it concerns harmful generated content, Guardrails is the content-policy control.

topics.title: PII: Macie vs. Comprehend vs. Guardrails
topics.rule: First locate the sensitive data: stored S3 objects, text processing, or model input/output.
topics.question: A company stores thousands of existing documents in Amazon S3. Before selecting files for a Bedrock Knowledge Base, security needs an inventory of eligible objects containing sensitive personal information and findings it can review. No model invocation is involved in this discovery step. The team has not yet selected the ingestion files. It needs discovery findings across the stored corpus, including a review of scan coverage, rather than only redaction of strings in future chat requests. Objects use supported formats. Which service is the best fit?
topics.clue: The target is sensitive-data discovery across existing S3 objects at rest.
topics.why: Use Amazon Macie to inspect eligible S3 objects and produce sensitive-data findings. Review both findings and scan coverage before approving ingestion candidates. Macie identifies data; the ingestion process must separately quarantine or sanitize files when policy requires it.

options.name: Amazon Macie
options.when: Discover/classify sensitive information in eligible S3 objects.
options.trap: A finding does not automatically rewrite or sanitize the object.
options.action: Run Macie discovery on eligible S3 objects, review findings and coverage, and approve files for the ingestion pipeline.

options.name: Amazon Comprehend
options.when: Detect PII/entities in a text preprocessing pipeline.
options.trap: Detection and verified redaction are separate operations.
options.wrong: Checking future response text does not inventory the existing S3 source objects before ingestion.
options.action: Add Comprehend PII detection to generated response processing after the entire corpus has been ingested.

options.name: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
options.when: Block/mask supported sensitive information in model interactions.
options.trap: Inline model safety is not a scan of a whole S3 corpus.
options.wrong: Invocation-time content checks do not perform the requested at-rest scan of the document corpus.
options.action: Apply a sensitive-information Guardrail to chat inputs and outputs and retain its interaction findings.

options.name: IAM access analysis
options.action: Audit S3 bucket IAM permissions and access logs before approving the existing files for ingestion.
options.when: IAM controls who can access resources.
options.trap: Access policy is not an inspection of object content.
options.wrong: Bucket permissions do not determine which stored documents contain sensitive personal data.

flow: Amazon S3: existing source objects
Amazon Macie: discover sensitive data in eligible objects
Security review: inspect findings and scan coverage
Ingestion approval: quarantine or sanitize before indexing as required
topics.change: Use Comprehend for supported PII detection in a text-processing pipeline, or Guardrails for supported sensitive-information handling at model interaction boundaries.

topics.title: CloudTrail vs. invocation logs vs. Config
topics.rule: Caller evidence, interaction content, and resource compliance answer different questions.
topics.question: A Bedrock application has CloudTrail enabled. After a harmful answer is reported, investigators can identify the invoking role but cannot reconstruct the actual prompt and response. Security also needs to retain the evidence under its content-log access policy. Token counts and API timestamps are available, but the actual words are not. The selected model operation supports invocation logging in the application Region. For future supported invocations, which additional configuration most directly captures the interaction content they need?
topics.clue: Caller audit evidence exists; the missing evidence is model input and output content.
topics.why: Enable Bedrock Model Invocation Logging for the relevant Region and supported invocation path, with protected CloudWatch Logs or S3 destinations. It captures supported input/output content for investigation. CloudTrail helps correlate the principal and API activity but is not the content log required here.

options.name: Bedrock Model Invocation Logging
options.when: Inspect supported model request/response content and invocation metadata.
options.trap: Disabled by default; sensitive content needs its own access and retention controls.
options.action: Enable Bedrock Model Invocation Logging for the supported path and retain its input/output records in protected destinations.

options.name: AWS CloudTrail
options.when: Identify who called which AWS API, when, and from where.
options.trap: API caller evidence is not a full prompt/response archive.
options.wrong: API audit events can identify callers and operations, but are not a substitute for the supported model input/output logging requested.
options.action: Expand CloudTrail event capture and retain model API activity with the existing principal and request metadata.

options.name: AWS Config
options.when: Inspect supported resource configuration/history and compliance checks.
options.trap: Configuration compliance is not per-prompt forensic capture.
options.wrong: Configuration history describes resource state rather than the content of a model interaction.
options.action: Enable Config recording and retain changes to the application’s model and logging resource configurations.

options.name: CloudWatch metrics
options.action: Retain CloudWatch input/output token metrics and correlate their timestamps with the known caller audit events.
options.when: Metrics measure counts, durations, and other operational signals.
options.trap: Aggregate measurements are not interaction content.
options.wrong: Token totals and latency do not reveal the actual words in the input or response.

flow: Bedrock Runtime: execute a supported invocation
Invocation logging: capture supported prompt and response data
CloudWatch Logs / S3: retain the protected content record
Investigation: correlate the content record with caller audit evidence
topics.change: If investigators only need who invoked or changed a resource, use CloudTrail; if they need historical resource configuration, use Config.

topics.title: SCPs vs. boundaries vs. IAM grants
topics.rule: Applicable ceilings constrain permissions; they do not grant them.
topics.question: An AWS Organizations member-account OU contains several application accounts. Security must prevent principals governed by the organization’s policies from invoking an unapproved Bedrock model, even when an account administrator adds an IAM allow. The requirement covers the governed principals in every member account in the OU, including roles created later. The organization needs prevention before a denied invocation occurs, rather than a spending alert afterward. Which control provides the organization-level preventive ceiling?
topics.clue: The denial must apply across the governed member accounts and override local permission grants.
topics.why: Attach an applicable SCP deny to the OU or accounts for the unapproved model access. An SCP limits the permissions available to governed principals; local IAM allows cannot override its explicit deny. The SCP does not itself grant access to approved models.

options.name: AWS Organizations SCP
options.when: Constrain applicable permissions across member accounts/OUs.
options.trap: SCPs do not grant permissions and do not govern every principal/account without exceptions.
options.action: Apply an SCP deny for the unapproved model to the OU/accounts and maintain identity grants for permitted access.

options.name: IAM permissions boundary
options.when: Limit the maximum permissions of that particular IAM entity.
options.trap: A role-level boundary is not automatically an organization-wide policy.
options.wrong: Boundaries on current roles do not provide the required OU-wide ceiling for future governed principals under local administration.
options.action: Set permissions boundaries on the current application roles and keep role-boundary assignment under account-local administration.

options.name: IAM identity policy
options.when: Grant permissions within applicable policies and ceilings.
options.trap: An allow is not the organization-level preventive restriction.
options.wrong: Approved-model allows on current roles can be changed or supplemented locally, so they do not supply the preventive organization ceiling.
options.action: Replace current application IAM grants with approved-model allow lists and let account administrators manage later role grants.

options.name: Detective IAM remediation
options.action: Use CloudTrail detection and an automated remediation process to remove unapproved model permissions after they are granted.
options.when: Detect and correct unintended permission changes as a supporting control.
options.trap: A reactive correction is not a preventive authorization ceiling.
options.wrong: Detection/remediation is reactive and leaves a gap before access is removed; the requirement is prevention despite local grants.

flow: OU / member accounts: establish the policy scope
Applicable SCP: deny unapproved model access
Identity policies: grant permitted access within the ceiling
Bedrock authorization: reject a request covered by an explicit deny
topics.change: Use a permissions boundary when the requirement is a ceiling for particular identities, such as delegated role creation, rather than an OU-wide policy.

topics.title: Config vs. GuardDuty vs. Security Hub
topics.rule: Configuration rules, supported threats, and aggregated findings are different evidence sources.
topics.question: A company stores Bedrock application logs in S3. Security requires a continuous compliance record showing whether the bucket’s supported configuration matches its encryption and public-access rules. It needs resource configuration history and rule-compliance results. Audit reviewers must see the configuration that was evaluated and the compliance outcome after changes. The absence of a detected attack is not sufficient evidence. The bucket and required checks are supported by the proposed recording/rule approach. Which service is the most direct fit?
topics.clue: The evidence required is resource configuration and compliance with configuration rules.
topics.why: Use AWS Config recording with appropriate managed or custom rules for the specified configuration requirements. Config tracks resource state and evaluates rule compliance. Threat detection and finding aggregation answer related security questions, but do not replace this configuration-compliance record.

options.name: AWS Config + appropriate rules
options.when: Record/evaluate supported resource configuration against policies.
options.trap: Custom rules or other checks may be required for unsupported settings.
options.action: Record the S3 bucket in Config and evaluate the required encryption/access configuration with appropriate rules.

options.name: Amazon GuardDuty
options.when: Detect supported threats or suspicious activity using its data sources.
options.trap: Threat detection is not every encryption/configuration compliance check.
options.wrong: A resource can be misconfigured without triggering a detected threat; no threat finding is not proof of rule compliance.
options.action: Enable GuardDuty threat detection and use its security findings to assess the log bucket.

options.name: AWS Security Hub
options.when: Aggregate supported security findings and posture checks.
options.trap: Aggregation is not identical to the underlying rule evaluator.
options.wrong: Aggregating findings does not itself create the specific configuration evaluation and history requested.
options.action: Aggregate the existing service findings in Security Hub without configuring the required bucket-compliance source controls.

options.name: CloudTrail caller audit
options.action: Retain CloudTrail bucket-change events and review the API activity as the required compliance result.
options.when: CloudTrail records API activity and associated caller evidence.
options.trap: An API event is not a configuration-rule evaluation.
options.wrong: Change events can support an audit, but do not supply the requested Config-style rule results.

flow: S3 log bucket: resource configuration
AWS Config recorder: track supported configuration changes
Config rules: evaluate encryption and access requirements
Compliance record: review findings and configuration history
topics.change: Choose GuardDuty for detected suspicious activity, or Security Hub when the requirement is to consolidate and manage security findings from supported controls and services.

topics.title: Direct vs. indirect prompt injection
topics.rule: Untrusted instructions can enter through user text, retrieved documents, or tool results.
topics.question: A Bedrock agent retrieves a maintenance manual from a Knowledge Base. The user asked a harmless repair question, but the manual contains instructions to ignore the task and send customer records to an external address. The agent also has data-access tools. The retrieved document is correctly cited and accessible to the user, so its source location and read permission are valid. The proposed export destination is not approved. The defense must remain effective even if the model follows the embedded instruction. Which response best addresses the attack’s entry point and its potential impact?
topics.clue: The malicious instruction entered through retrieved content, and the threatened impact is an unauthorized tool action.
topics.why: Treat the retrieved manual as untrusted data and constrain tool access with deterministic authorization and approved destinations. This is indirect prompt injection because the instruction arrived through an external source rather than the user request. Applicable input checks add protection, but a prompt instruction alone cannot enforce the tool boundary.

options.name: Untrusted retrieval + tool authorization
options.when: Attacker instructions are embedded in material the application supplies as evidence.
options.trap: Filtering only the user message leaves another input surface.
options.action: Treat retrieved text as untrusted and reject tool calls outside the caller’s data scope or approved destinations in the handler.

options.name: User-message filtering
options.when: Inspect attacks entering in a user request.
options.trap: Later retrieved or tool-provided text is a separate untrusted entry point.
options.wrong: The original message is harmless; the attack arrives later through retrieval and is not covered by that user-only check.
options.action: Strengthen user-input injection filtering and trust retrieved passages that pass identity-based document access checks.

options.name: System prompt instructions
options.when: Describe desired model behavior and evidence-use rules.
options.trap: Instructions cannot replace deterministic enforcement of tool authority.
options.wrong: A behavioral instruction does not enforce data-access or destination policy when a model proposes a tool call.
options.action: Strengthen the agent’s system instruction and rely on it to reject the export before invoking the broadly authorized tool.

options.name: Citation-based trust
options.action: Require a source citation for every tool proposal and allow cited instructions from authorized retrieved documents.
options.when: Citations identify source locations for evidence review.
options.trap: Source attribution does not authorize instructions or data exports.
options.wrong: A real source can contain hostile text; its citation does not make the requested export permitted.

flow: Knowledge Bases retrieval: obtain a manual as untrusted evidence
Context handling: separate source text from instructions and apply relevant checks
Bedrock agent: produce a proposed answer or tool call
Tool handler: enforce permitted data scope and destinations
topics.change: If the malicious instruction is submitted directly by the user, it is direct injection; tool authorization is still needed whenever actions can affect protected data.

topics.title: RAG retrieval vs. contextual grounding checks
topics.rule: Retrieval supplies evidence before generation; grounding checks assess supported response/source alignment.
topics.question: A Bedrock assistant retrieves the current policy correctly. The model’s answer adds an eligibility claim that is absent from the supplied passage. The team wants to check completed answers against the source and route failed checks to a safe fallback before returning them. Traces confirm that the full relevant passage reached the model and that the output satisfies the required JSON schema. Increasing retrieval count has not removed the unsupported claim. The required source-based response-check feature is available for the selected configuration. Which capability best targets this requirement?
topics.clue: Retrieval succeeded; the requirement is a post-generation source-support check.
topics.why: Configure supported Bedrock Guardrails contextual grounding checks using the source, query, and generated response. The check evaluates grounding/relevance against the supplied context and can support the application’s block or fallback policy. It addresses unsupported claims after retrieval rather than changing API access permissions.

options.name: Bedrock Guardrails contextual grounding checks
options.when: Assess supported generated response/source alignment and relevance.
options.trap: Scores are not calibrated truth probabilities and support limits matter.
options.action: Run a supported contextual grounding check using the source and answer, then apply the block/fallback policy before delivery.

options.name: Knowledge Bases retrieval alone
options.when: Supply authorized relevant evidence before generation.
options.trap: Correct context does not guarantee faithful generation.
options.wrong: Additional passages do not perform the requested post-generation comparison of claims with their supporting evidence.
options.action: Increase Knowledge Bases result count and rely on the expanded evidence set to prevent unsupported output.

options.name: IAM invoke permission
options.when: Authorize AWS model calls.
options.trap: API access control does not assess factual support.
options.wrong: Invoke authorization establishes API permission, not whether the response is supported by the policy.
options.action: Restrict IAM model access and treat successful model authorization as sufficient to release the answer.

options.name: Output schema validation
options.action: Enforce the output schema and require citations to retrieved passages before releasing the answer.
options.when: Schema checks enforce structure and allowed field types.
options.trap: A well-formed claim can still be unsupported.
options.wrong: Valid structure and real citations can accompany unsupported claims; this does not implement the requested grounding check.

flow: Knowledge Bases: retrieve the approved policy passage
Amazon Bedrock: generate the proposed answer
Contextual grounding check: assess source support and query relevance
Application policy: return the answer or use a safe fallback
topics.change: If the needed policy passage never reaches generation, investigate retrieval coverage or context assembly before treating the defect as grounded-generation validation.

name: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications
summary: Match caching, token parameters, capacity, traffic control, and observability to the actual bottleneck.

topics.title: Semantic vs. prompt vs. fingerprint caching
topics.rule: The reusable unit determines the cache: equivalent answer, identical prefix processing, or exact scoped request/result.
topics.question: A Bedrock application sends the same long system policy before different user questions. The selected model supports prompt caching and the policy meets its checkpoint requirements. Answers must be generated for each question rather than reused. User questions are intentionally different and some ask for different decisions under the same policy. Permission and evidence checks still apply on every call. The goal is inference-prefix reuse during the cache lifetime, not returning an earlier answer. Which optimization most directly reduces repeated processing of the stable policy?
topics.clue: The prefix repeats exactly, but the questions and answers differ.
topics.why: Place a supported prompt-cache checkpoint after the stable policy. Bedrock can reuse processing for that matching prefix while processing each new question and generating its answer. Response caches reuse completed answers, so they address a different repeated-work pattern.

options.name: Bedrock prompt caching
options.when: An identical sufficiently long supported prefix repeats across requests.
options.trap: The suffix/output still needs inference; cache writes/reads have model-specific rules.
options.action: Cache the supported matching policy prefix with a Bedrock checkpoint and process each question to generate a fresh answer.

options.name: Semantic response caching
options.when: Equivalent authorized questions can reuse a current evaluated answer.
options.trap: Meaning similarity does not always establish equivalent facts/permissions.
options.wrong: An evaluated semantic response cache can be useful, but it reuses an answer rather than preserving the required per-question generation.
options.action: Use a semantic response cache scoped to identity and corpus version to return answers for similar incoming questions.

options.name: Exact result caching
options.when: The complete scoped request/configuration matches a valid stored result.
options.trap: Question-only hashes omit permissions/version; expiry/eviction can miss.
options.wrong: Exact result reuse is scoped and safe when keys match, but different question inputs do not share a complete request fingerprint.
options.action: Cache completed answers by the complete scoped request fingerprint and reuse matching results within a valid lifetime.

options.name: Lambda provisioned concurrency
options.action: Pre-initialize Lambda environments and reuse the in-memory system-policy string across invocations.
options.when: Provisioned concurrency reduces Lambda initialization delay.
options.trap: Application execution capacity is separate from model prefix processing.
options.wrong: Warm application memory avoids rebuilding local input; it does not reuse the model’s computation of the repeated prefix.

flow: Request: stable policy plus a new user question
Bedrock prompt-cache checkpoint: reuse eligible matching prefix processing
Inference: process the new suffix and generate an answer
Response: return the newly generated answer
topics.change: If the same authorized question can safely reuse a current answer, an exact or evaluated semantic response cache may fit; invalidate it when evidence or policy changes.

topics.title: Temperature vs. top-p vs. top-k
topics.rule: Sampling controls affect next-token selection; output limits affect length. None certifies truth.
topics.question: A team tunes a Bedrock text-generation model that supports temperature, top-p, and top-k. It wants each sampling step to consider no more than 20 candidate next tokens. It is not changing the output-length limit or the number of retrieved passages. The application already has separate response-length and retrieval-count settings. The team is comparing sampling behavior while keeping the model and input fixed, and needs a candidate-count bound rather than a probability-mass threshold. Which parameter directly expresses that requirement?
topics.clue: The limit is a count of candidate next tokens at each sampling step.
topics.why: Set the model’s supported top-k parameter to 20. Top-k limits the candidate token count, whereas top-p limits cumulative probability mass and temperature adjusts the distribution. This sampling choice does not guarantee factual correctness or valid output structure.

options.name: Model-specific top-k
options.when: Limit sampling to a configured number of candidate next tokens.
options.trap: Support and interactions vary by model; this does not guarantee valid JSON/facts.
options.action: Set the supported model-specific top-k parameter to 20 and retain the independent response-length setting.

options.name: Temperature
options.when: Adjust the sampling distribution/randomness where supported.
options.trap: Low temperature does not imply factual correctness or portable determinism.
options.wrong: Temperature changes sampling distribution/randomness rather than specifying a fixed candidate count.
options.action: Lower temperature while retaining the current top-k and response-length settings.

options.name: Top-p (nucleus sampling)
options.when: Restrict candidates by cumulative probability mass.
options.trap: It is a mass threshold, not a fixed number of tokens.
options.wrong: The number of candidates within a probability-mass threshold varies; top-p is not a fixed token count.
options.action: Set top-p to 0.9 while retaining the current top-k and response-length settings.

options.name: Maximum output tokens
options.action: Set the maximum generated output-token count to 20 while retaining the current sampling settings.
options.when: Limit the generated response length.
options.trap: Output length and per-step sampling candidates are different counts.
options.wrong: This caps the entire answer length, not the candidate set at each generation step.

flow: Bedrock request: specify supported sampling parameters
Top-k: retain at most 20 candidate next tokens
Sampling: choose the next token from the permitted set
Output validation: check structure and required facts
topics.change: Use top-p for a cumulative-probability threshold, temperature for distribution/randomness, or max-output tokens for a response-length bound.

topics.title: Lambda reserved vs. provisioned concurrency
topics.rule: Reserved concurrency allocates/caps executions; provisioned concurrency initializes environments.
topics.question: An API Gateway and Lambda application invokes Bedrock. Traces show that slow first requests spend most of the extra time initializing Lambda before the model call. Bedrock latency and capacity meet their targets. The function already has reserved concurrency high enough for the observed demand and shows no admission throttling. Later requests on initialized environments are fast. The team is willing to pay for prepared function capacity to meet startup latency targets. Which change most directly targets the measured delay?
topics.clue: The additional delay is Lambda initialization, before Bedrock inference begins.
topics.why: Configure Lambda provisioned concurrency for the expected request capacity so environments are initialized ahead of use. This targets the initialization stage identified in the trace. Size it for demand and monitor spillover, because requests beyond provisioned capacity can still use on-demand environments.

options.name: Lambda provisioned concurrency
options.when: Reduce initialization delay for configured Lambda capacity.
options.trap: It costs extra and does not eliminate every spillover cold start.
options.action: Configure Lambda provisioned concurrency for the expected request capacity and monitor initialization delay and spillover.

options.name: Lambda reserved concurrency
options.when: Allocate and cap a function’s concurrent executions.
options.trap: A concurrency reservation does not pre-initialize environments.
options.wrong: Reserved concurrency allocates and caps concurrent executions; it does not pre-initialize the configured environments.
options.action: Raise Lambda reserved concurrency above the current allocation and monitor concurrent execution counts.

options.name: Bedrock Provisioned Throughput
options.when: Reserve supported model capacity for measured demand.
options.trap: It does not pre-initialize Lambda.
options.wrong: The delay occurs before Bedrock, whose latency and capacity already meet the target.
options.action: Reserve Bedrock Provisioned Throughput and monitor model-side throughput and latency.

options.name: API timeout tuning
options.action: Extend the API Gateway timeout and monitor whether more first requests complete successfully.
options.when: Timeouts control how long the request can wait.
options.trap: A longer permitted wait does not remove initialization work.
options.wrong: The request may be allowed to run longer, but the measured startup delay remains.

flow: API Gateway: receive the request
Provisioned Lambda environment: avoid the targeted initialization wait
Amazon Bedrock: run the model invocation
Trace review: verify the initialization and total-latency change
topics.change: Use reserved concurrency to allocate or cap a function’s executions; evaluate model capacity when traces show model-side throttling or latency instead.

topics.title: CloudWatch vs. X-Ray vs. invocation logs
topics.rule: Trends, individual request paths, and interaction content require different telemetry.
topics.question: A Bedrock RAG application uses API Gateway, Lambda, and a retrieval service. Overall latency has increased, but aggregate metrics do not show whether retrieval or model invocation causes the delay for affected requests. Some requests have large retrieved contexts, while others have small contexts but slow vector queries. The team needs evidence for each affected request before changing model capacity or the search service; caller identity and token totals are already available. Which additional evidence best supports attributing latency to those stages?
topics.clue: The team needs per-request timing across retrieval and model-call boundaries.
topics.why: Instrument distributed traces with separate retrieval and model SDK spans and correlate them with each request. Their durations show which application stage consumes the time. Aggregate metrics show trends, and invocation logs show supported content, but neither alone supplies the requested stage timing.

options.name: X-Ray / OpenTelemetry distributed trace
options.when: Attribute time/failure across instrumented request stages.
options.trap: Tracing does not automatically expose uninstrumented or hidden model internals.
options.action: Add correlated retrieval and Bedrock SDK spans with OpenTelemetry/X-Ray and compare their durations in affected traces.

options.name: CloudWatch aggregate token metrics only
options.when: Monitor changing counts, latency distributions, errors, and alarms.
options.trap: An aggregate trend may not reconstruct this request’s individual path.
options.wrong: Input-token totals do not measure the elapsed time of this request’s retrieval and model stages.
options.action: Compare aggregate Bedrock token counts and API latency metrics over the same period to select the slower stage.

options.name: CloudTrail API caller event only
options.when: Establish the principal/API call and related audit evidence.
options.trap: Caller evidence is not a full distributed latency breakdown.
options.wrong: Caller audit events identify API activity but are not the requested instrumented application-stage trace.
options.action: Correlate CloudTrail caller audit events with request timestamps to reconstruct the complete retrieval/model stage timing.

options.name: Invocation content logging
options.action: Enable invocation content logging and inspect large prompts to assign the request’s retrieval and generation durations.
options.when: Inspect supported model input/output content.
options.trap: Interaction content does not by itself measure upstream retrieval time.
options.wrong: The prompt may reveal what was supplied, but not how long retrieval took in the application.

flow: API request: attach a correlation identifier
Retrieval span: measure evidence-fetch duration
Bedrock span: measure the model-call duration
Distributed trace: compare the stages for the affected request
topics.change: Use CloudWatch for aggregate trends and alarms, or invocation logs when the investigation needs the actual supported prompt/response content.

topics.title: SQS buffering vs. throttling vs. scaling
topics.rule: Queue excess work, reject excess requests, or expand eligible capacity: these solve different constraints.
topics.question: A document-analysis API receives bursts above the safe Bedrock invocation rate. Each accepted submission must be retained. Callers can receive a job ID and retrieve results later. The model quota cannot be increased immediately. A traffic spike lasts several minutes, and a successful API acknowledgment must mean the work is durably accepted. Workers can scale, but more workers cannot raise the current downstream quota. Results must remain accessible by the submitted job identifier. Which architecture best absorbs the bursts without losing accepted work?
topics.clue: Accepted work must be retained while execution is paced below a fixed downstream rate.
topics.why: Put accepted jobs in SQS and drain them with workers that enforce the model’s applicable request/token rate and bounded concurrency. The queue decouples admission from completion and retains excess work. Scaling workers or rejecting excess requests alone does not meet both retention and safe model-rate requirements.

options.name: SQS + paced Lambda/container workers
options.when: Durably queue work when asynchronous completion is acceptable.
options.trap: A queue alone does not implement a token-rate limiter.
options.action: Acknowledge durably queued SQS jobs, then drain them with rate-controlled workers and persist results by job identifier.

options.name: API Gateway throttling alone
options.when: Reject excess admission to protect the downstream path.
options.trap: Rejected requests are not automatically persisted as jobs.
options.wrong: Throttles can reject excess requests, but acknowledgment before durable acceptance does not meet the promised retention of accepted jobs.
options.action: Acknowledge requests immediately, then invoke Bedrock synchronously and use API throttles to shed excess work.

options.name: Application Auto Scaling alone
options.when: Eligible worker/endpoint capacity should scale with demand.
options.trap: More workers cannot override a fixed downstream model quota.
options.wrong: Dispatch and scaling without durable buffering/rate control do not preserve accepted work or protect the fixed downstream quota.
options.action: Acknowledge requests after dispatching them to an autoscaled worker fleet and let each worker invoke Bedrock independently.

options.name: Synchronous retry loop
options.action: Acknowledge requests after starting in-memory retries and keep retrying model throttles until a worker succeeds.
options.when: Use bounded backoff for transient failures within a request budget.
options.trap: Unbounded immediate retries amplify overload and do not create durable jobs.
options.wrong: In-memory retries are not durable acceptance and can amplify overload; losing the worker can lose an acknowledged submission.

flow: Submission API: persist the job and return its identifier
Amazon SQS: buffer accepted work
Paced workers: invoke Bedrock within the downstream rate
Result store: persist completion for authorized later retrieval
topics.change: If callers require immediate completion and rejected requests are acceptable, admission throttling can fit; if downstream capacity can grow, scaling may complement the queue.

topics.title: Cost Explorer vs. Budgets vs. token alarms
topics.rule: Billing analysis, budget notifications, and runtime token alarms use different measurements.
topics.question: Operations wants an alert when the Bedrock InputTokenCount metric exceeds a defined threshold over a five-minute interval. The alert must use the operational metric rather than wait for a monthly cost report. Billing analysis already supports the monthly financial review. This additional control is intended to detect an operational surge during the day. The team has chosen the metric statistic and wants notifications through its existing alarm-response process. Which service should own this alarm?
topics.clue: The trigger is a threshold on an emitted runtime metric over a specified interval.
